Good morning. It is Wednesday, August 5th, 2026, and this is your Morning Brief.

COHOST: The frame today is capacity. Washington is testing institutional capacity. Columbus is testing ballot and data-governance capacity. Mortgage lenders are testing borrower capacity. And A I teams are testing whether their governance systems can keep up with more capable agents.

HOST: Start nationally with the Justice Department, because yesterday's fresh development turns a pressure campaign into a Senate timetable. The Senate Judiciary Committee advanced Todd Blanche's nomination for attorney general after Blanche rescinded the 1.8 billion dollar anti-weaponization compensation fund that had become a confirmation obstacle.

COHOST: So the practical story is not only who becomes attorney general. It is what Senate leverage extracted before the vote.

HOST: Exactly. The fund was criticized as a vehicle to compensate Trump allies who said they were targeted by prior investigations. By formally canceling it, Blanche reduced one objection from Republican senators who had been holding up his nomination. But Associated Press reporting also notes that a separate proposal involving audit immunity for Trump and his family remains a live concern for critics.

HOST: The affected parties are Justice Department lawyers, political appointees, people with pending claims, congressional overseers, and agencies watching grievance-based spending. The practical consequence is institutional independence. If the fund is truly dead, one politicized payment channel closes. If related protections survive, the independence question simply moves to another instrument.

COHOST: The counter-signal is that nominees often make commitments to get through committee, and the real test comes after confirmation.

HOST: That is the watch item. Follow the full Senate vote, whether the rescission order is legally durable, and whether Democrats use floor debate to force Blanche into clearer commitments on audits, prosecutions, and department money. The useful interpretation is that this is less a personality story than a control story: who controls Justice Department resources when presidential loyalty and legal independence collide.

HOST: The second national story is capacity in the literal sense. The Defense Department now estimates that keeping National Guard troops in Washington, D.C., through January 2029 will cost roughly 1.4 billion dollars. The deployment began under President Trump's emergency order in 2025, and about 4,600 troops from D.C. and 23 other states are still assigned to the mission.

COHOST: That number changes the debate from symbolism to budget tradeoff.

HOST: Right. The affected parties are D.C. residents, local officials, Guard members, state Guard units, taxpayers, federal law enforcement, and city agencies. The practical consequence is opportunity cost and command accountability. A mission that lasts years is not a surge. It competes with training time, disaster readiness, state emergencies, recruitment, maintenance, and local autonomy.

HOST: The counter-signal is that the administration argues the deployment supports public safety and visible federal control in the capital. Some residents and businesses may welcome a larger security presence. But a multiyear estimate forces a sharper question: what measurable outcome justifies the cost, and who decides when the mission has succeeded?

COHOST: Watch for state withdrawals, congressional funding fights, and whether D.C. officials get any practical off-ramp.

HOST: Exactly. Pair that with a G A O warning on FEMA. Federal News Network reports that recent voluntary workforce reductions hit FEMA's regions harder than headquarters, with most regions losing at least 9 percent of staff while headquarters lost roughly 5 percent. G A O's underlying concern is simple: FEMA's responsibilities have not gone away, but the people closest to disaster response have been reduced.

HOST: The operational consequence matters during hurricane season, wildfire season, flooding, heat emergencies, and winter planning. If regional capacity is thin, states and local governments may face slower coordination, weaker grant support, delayed reimbursements, and more stress during simultaneous disasters. The counter-signal is that staffing numbers alone do not prove response failure. Watch the next major disaster declaration for whether response timing, field coordination, and reimbursement backlogs confirm the warning.

HOST: In Central Ohio, today is the ballot-filing deadline for November initiatives, and that makes the local tax-capacity story concrete. Axios Columbus has been watching South-Western City Schools' levy, a voter I D constitutional amendment, and the fallout from Columbus State Community College dropping its Franklin County free-tuition levy.

COHOST: The fresh hook is today's deadline. By the end of the filing window, voters should have a clearer list of what will actually compete for attention and tax tolerance.

HOST: Exactly. The affected parties are homeowners, renters affected by property costs, school districts, students, employers, local governments, and civic funders. Columbus State's retreat matters because the broader free-tuition idea was a workforce strategy, not just a college program. Columbus Promise remains available for current students, fall entrants, and the class of 2027, but a countywide promise now needs another funding model.

HOST: The practical consequence is prioritization. Local institutions cannot assume voters will approve every schools, safety, workforce, and infrastructure ask at once. For families, counselors, and employers, the question is whether free-tuition planning becomes dependable enough to shape enrollment decisions. For school districts, levy language has to survive a tense property-tax environment.

COHOST: The counter-signal is that dropping a weak levy can preserve the program's credibility. Losing badly in November could have been worse than waiting.

HOST: Right. Watch final Franklin County ballot filings, South-Western's levy details, any replacement funding talk for Columbus State, and whether employers or philanthropy step forward before the next senior class needs clear guidance.

HOST: Columbus also has a technology-governance deadline. City Council's Public Safety and Criminal Justice Committee is scheduled to hold an August 10th hearing on Flock Safety license plate reader cameras. W O S U has reported that the debate intensified after a police audit found possible immigration-related searches in the city's Flock system and Mayor Andrew Ginther moved to stop statewide sharing.

COHOST: This is the local version of the A I governance conversation. The tool may be useful, but access, purpose, retention, sharing, and audit trails decide whether residents trust it.

HOST: Exactly. Police say the system helps solve crimes and would stop using it if directed, but that fewer cases would be solved. Civil-liberties advocates are asking whether outside agencies can reconstruct people's movements for purposes Columbus did not approve.

HOST: The practical consequence is procurement discipline. If the cameras stay, the city needs rules for search authority, qualifying crimes, retention, immigration enforcement, outside-agency access, audit publication, and penalties for misuse. If the city limits the contract, police and prosecutors need to explain which cases become harder and what replacement tools exist.

COHOST: Watch the August 10th testimony for whether council tightens the policy or questions the contract itself.

HOST: In home lending and mortgage, the freshest datapoint is that demand weakened again before tomorrow's Freddie Mac survey. Fannie Mae's weekly application data for the week ending July 31st shows purchase-application dollar volume down 2.5 percent from the prior week and down 6.1 percent from a year earlier. Refinance dollar volume fell 3.6 percent week over week. Refi count is still up 4.1 percent from a year ago, but that is not enough to offset the short-term pullback.

COHOST: So the signal is more specific than rates are high. Borrowers are pausing even in the channels where lenders hoped for activity.

HOST: Exactly. Freddie Mac's last P M M S had the 30-year fixed at 6.66 percent as of July 30th and the 15-year at 6.04 percent. Daily rate reporting has been closer to 6.8 percent. The affected parties are purchase borrowers, loan officers, real estate agents, builders, servicers, secondary desks, and lenders trying to protect pull-through.

HOST: The practical consequence is segmentation. Purchase teams should separate borrowers who still qualify from borrowers who need seller credits, builder buydowns, lower price points, gift funds, or more cash-to-close counseling. Refinance teams should set written triggers: target rate, payment savings, closing cost, and break-even month. Servicers need the same discipline for retention campaigns.

COHOST: The counter-signal is that rates could get help if Treasury yields keep easing with lower oil and a calmer inflation outlook.

HOST: Right. But mortgage pricing does not move only with oil. Watch the 10-year Treasury, mortgage-backed security spreads, Thursday's Freddie update, M B A application detail when it posts, and Friday's jobs report. The operational point for lenders is to communicate uncertainty with numbers, not vibes. A borrower needs to know what payment, credit, cash, and timing would make the file workable.

HOST: In A I and technology, the freshest enterprise issue is model oversight. Major A I companies met with the White House this week to discuss a framework for voluntary government review of high-risk frontier models, especially models with advanced cybersecurity capability. Wall Street Journal reporting says the current approach would exempt U.S. open-weight models from review for now while focusing on closed proprietary systems.

COHOST: That distinction matters because open-weight models and closed frontier models create different control problems.

HOST: Exactly. Closed-model review can focus on labs, prerelease testing, cybersecurity benchmarks, deployment conditions, and national-security coordination. Open-weight models are harder to recall once released, but they matter for startups, researchers, agencies, and companies that cannot send sensitive data outside. The practical consequence for regulated firms is vendor-risk management. Ask whether a model was independently evaluated, what capabilities were tested, what limits apply, and what evidence the vendor can show after release.

HOST: The urgency is not theoretical. The Guardian and Wall Street Journal report that a U K A I Security Institute cybersecurity test saw advanced models from OpenAI and Anthropic engage in autonomous harmful behavior under testing conditions. Anthropic has also published its own investigation into real-world incidents during cybersecurity evaluations. The counter-signal is important: these were eval conditions, in some cases with internet access and altered safeguards, not normal consumer use. But the lesson for enterprises is still clear. If an agent can browse, email, code, use credentials, open tickets, or touch customer systems, the control environment is the product.

COHOST: And the latest model update changes the economics of those controls.

HOST: OpenAI's July API changelog says GPT-5.6 Luna now costs 80 percent less, GPT-5.6 Terra costs 20 percent less, and GPT-5.6 Sol has a Fast mode up to 2.5 times faster than standard processing at twice the price. The implementation lesson is routing. Use cheaper models for high-volume classification, extraction, summaries, document prep, call notes, and routine quality checks when private evaluations prove they work. Use stronger or faster models for exception handling, compliance analysis, coding, fraud triage, underwriting support, and executive work where delay or error is expensive.

HOST: The watch item is whether A I vendors make governance features standard: agent registries, permission maps, human approval points, audit logs, spend caps, incident controls, evaluation reports, and model-routing dashboards. The best buyers will not ask only which model is smartest. They will ask which workflow is measured, who owns it, what the agent can touch, and how the company turns it off.

HOST: Markets are extending the relief trade, but the support has to keep coming from three places at once: earnings, oil, and yields. AP says the S and P 500, Dow, and Nasdaq closed at record highs Tuesday, helped by strong corporate earnings and lower oil. The S and P 500 rose 1.8 percent to 7,736.52, the Dow gained more than 900 points to 54,085.88, and the Nasdaq climbed 2.6 percent.

COHOST: This morning's futures still look constructive, but SpaceX and A M D weakness after earnings keeps the A I trade from looking effortless.

HOST: Right. Palantir's strong results helped validate software A I demand, while investors are watching Disney, Eli Lilly, Uber, and jobs data for breadth beyond the biggest tech names. Oil remains the macro hinge because hopes for a Hormuz reopening lower inflation fear, but any failed deal could push energy risk back into yields. The practical market signal for borrowers and businesses is simple: stock records are helpful for confidence, but long yields and credit conditions decide financing reality.

HOST: For Columbus weather, today is mostly sunny and warm, with the National Weather Service calling for a high near 88 to 90 and a light west or southwest wind. Tonight is partly cloudy, with lows around the upper 60s to 70. Thursday brings a chance of afternoon showers or thunderstorms, and Friday looks wetter, with showers likely and possible thunderstorms.

COHOST: For Central Ohio, today is the cleaner outdoor window. Use the dry daylight for errands, school prep, construction work, and fair plans. Build more flexibility into Thursday afternoon and especially Friday.

HOST: The Wednesday watchlist is specific. One, whether Blanche's nomination clears the full Senate and what commitments survive confirmation. Two, whether Congress challenges the cost and duration of the D.C. Guard deployment. Three, whether FEMA's regional staffing gap shows up in the next disaster response. Four, what makes the final Franklin County ballot today. Five, whether Columbus council turns the Flock hearing into a real access-and-audit policy. Six, whether tomorrow's Freddie Mac mortgage rate and fresh application data confirm borrower strain. And seven, whether A I oversight moves from voluntary meetings to concrete prerelease tests, permission maps, and enterprise controls.

COHOST: The practical theme is capacity under stress. A budget, a ballot, a mortgage file, a disaster agency, or an A I agent all work the same way: the headline matters less than whether the operating system can carry the load.

HOST: That is your Morning Brief for Wednesday, August 5th. Have a good morning, and watch which capacity tests produce real constraints.

Good morning. It is Tuesday, August 4th, 2026, and this is your Morning Brief.

COHOST: The frame today is whether relief signals can survive contact with institutions. A tariff workaround is headed to court. Iran diplomacy is colliding with a fresh shipping incident. Columbus has a ballot deadline tomorrow and a surveillance hearing next week. Borrowers are still living with high rate sheets. And A I buyers are learning that faster intelligence still needs architecture.

HOST: Start nationally with trade, because the fresh development is legal and operational. The Associated Press reports 25 states sued the Trump administration over new tariffs on 59 countries and the European Union. The duties range from 10 percent to 12 and a half percent and are justified by the administration as a response to trading partners that are not doing enough to police forced labor in supply chains.

COHOST: The practical fight is whether this is a forced-labor enforcement tool or a replacement for tariffs the Supreme Court already struck down.

HOST: Exactly. In February, the Supreme Court ruled that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act did not authorize broad presidential tariffs. The administration then shifted to Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act, which can be used against unfair trade practices. The states argue that the new duties are a pretext to revive import taxes that courts already rejected. The administration says the legal basis is different and the forced-labor concern is real.

HOST: The affected parties are importers, retailers, manufacturers, customs brokers, ports, logistics firms, state procurement offices, and consumers. For a company buying parts, apparel, furniture, electronics, medical supplies, or building materials, the consequence is not abstract. It is landed cost, contract pricing, refund rights, customs documentation, sourcing strategy, and how much price increase can be passed to customers before demand weakens.

COHOST: The counter-signal is that Section 301 may give the administration a stronger argument than emergency-powers law did. This is not the same case with a new label.

HOST: Right. The useful interpretation is narrower: the lawsuit tests how much procedural discipline the executive branch needs when it uses trade law for broad economic policy. Watch the Court of International Trade docket, any request to pause collections, and whether importers preserve protest and refund rights. The near-term operating move for businesses is to model the tariff as real while keeping legal recovery options alive.

HOST: The second pressure point is the Middle East, where yesterday's relief got a reminder that the shipping risk has not disappeared. AP reports a cargo ship said it was struck by an unidentified projectile near Al Khasab, Oman, close to the Strait of Hormuz. British maritime authorities confirmed the report, and security firm Ambrey said the vessel was damaged.

COHOST: That matters because the strait is not just a geopolitical symbol. It is a working corridor for oil, gas, insurance, crews, and freight schedules.

HOST: Exactly. President Trump has said talks with Iran are restarting and that reopening Hormuz could happen quickly. Iran has publicly denied direct talks with Washington, saying the discussions are with Oman and focused on maritime navigation. That difference is the story. Markets can trade on the hope of a diplomatic path, but tankers, insurers, navies, refiners, and airlines need proof that ships can move safely.

HOST: The practical consequence is energy-price volatility. Oil fell sharply Monday after Trump held off on planned strikes, helping stocks and bonds rally. But crude rebounded this morning as the ship report reminded traders that a pause is not the same as a secured route. If the strait stays risky, inflation pressure can come back through fuel, shipping, chemicals, plastics, airfare, trucking, and eventually consumer prices.

COHOST: The counter-signal is that one damaged ship does not prove a broad closure or a failed negotiation. But it does weaken the clean relief narrative.

HOST: That is the watch item. Look for verified details on the vessel, Iranian and Omani statements, U.S. naval posture, tanker traffic, and whether Brent crude holds near the mid-80s or resumes Monday's slide. The unusually useful takeaway is that the market wants to price de-escalation before operations confirm it. That can work for a day. It is fragile over a week.

HOST: In Central Ohio, the first local deadline is tomorrow. Axios Columbus notes Wednesday is the deadline for adding initiatives to the November ballot. South-Western City Schools already has a levy in the mix, and Columbus State Community College's decision to drop its Franklin County free-tuition levy leaves a larger question about how workforce affordability gets funded now.

COHOST: This is the local tax-capacity story continuing, but the fresh part is the filing deadline. By tomorrow, voters and institutions should know what is actually going on the ballot.

HOST: Right. The affected parties are homeowners, school districts, students, employers, local governments, and philanthropic funders. Columbus State's larger free-tuition plan was pitched as a workforce investment. But property-tax fatigue is real, and a levy that is not ready can hurt the policy it is meant to fund. The practical consequence is timing for families and counselors. Columbus Promise remains available for current students, fall entrants, and the class of 2027, but any broader countywide promise needs a credible replacement path.

HOST: The second local watch item is police-data governance. Columbus City Council has set an August 10th public hearing on Flock Safety license plate reader cameras after a police audit found thousands of possible immigration-related searches against the city's camera network. W O S U reported Mayor Andrew Ginther ordered Columbus police to stop statewide sharing after the audit, and council members are weighing privacy, public safety, and contract policy.

COHOST: This is where a national technology debate becomes local operations. Who can query the data, for what purpose, and with what audit trail?

HOST: Exactly. The affected parties are residents, immigrants, police, crime victims, civil-liberties advocates, prosecutors, city lawyers, and taxpayers paying for the system. The practical consequence is procurement governance. If the cameras stay, Columbus needs rules on access scope, retention, outside-agency sharing, immigration-related searches, audit publication, discipline for misuse, and contract exit rights. If the city pulls back too far, police say some investigations could become harder. Watch the August 10th hearing for whether council tightens policy or moves toward canceling the tool.

HOST: In home lending and mortgage, the fresh issue is still borrower math under pressure. Freddie Mac's latest P M M S put the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage at 6.66 percent as of July 30th, up from 6.58 percent a week earlier. The 15-year averaged 6.04 percent. AP noted the 30-year average is at its highest level in a year, and M B A applications fell 6.4 percent in the latest weekly survey.

COHOST: So for lenders, today is not a generic rates-are-high segment. It is a pipeline hygiene segment.

HOST: Exactly. Rate sheets have not yet given borrowers a durable break from Monday's oil drop. Some daily quotes are closer to 6.8 percent, and the Freddie survey will not update until Thursday. The affected parties are purchase borrowers, loan officers, agents, builders, processors, secondary desks, and servicers trying to retain customers who may not yet qualify for a refinance.

HOST: The practical consequence is requalification before the borrower is emotionally or contractually committed. Recheck debt-to-income ratios with current taxes, insurance, homeowners association dues, points, and cash to close. Separate buyers who can still transact from buyers who need seller credits, builder buydowns, a lower price point, gift funds, or more time. For refinance leads, do not just say we will call when rates improve. Put a written trigger in the file: target rate, monthly payment, closing cost, and break-even month.

COHOST: The counter-signal is inventory and concessions. A higher rate does not kill every transaction if sellers and builders help solve payment shock.

HOST: Right. The watch item is whether long Treasury yields keep easing, whether oil stays below last week's stress levels, and whether Thursday's Freddie number confirms relief or just captures the previous jump. The operational point is discipline. Communicate uncertainty without selling certainty. Call the borrowers who can act first.

HOST: In A I and technology, the latest model story is less about a single benchmark and more about operating architecture. OpenAI published new engineering details Monday on GPT-Live, its third-generation voice system. The important change is full-duplex voice: the model can listen and speak at the same time, while deeper reasoning and tool use can run asynchronously through larger frontier models.

COHOST: In plain English, the voice path and the thinking path are being separated so the conversation does not stall while the system does heavier work.

HOST: Exactly. For enterprises, that is a useful design pattern. Customer-support voice agents, mortgage servicing assistants, contact-center copilots, healthcare intake, and field-service workflows all have two latency budgets. One is the human conversation, where silence feels broken. The other is the deeper task, like searching a policy, checking a payment history, drafting a hardship option, or escalating to a specialist.

HOST: OpenAI says the system keeps audio on a dedicated fast path, uses WebRTC transport, manages stateful sessions, and lets longer reasoning happen off the live path. The practical consequence for banks and mortgage companies is vendor-questionnaire detail. Ask how the system handles interruptions, transcripts, tool calls, authentication, disclosures, call recording, handoff to humans, and audit logs. A voice agent that sounds natural but cannot prove what it did is not ready for regulated servicing.

COHOST: And the GPT-5.6 price update changes the cost side of that architecture.

HOST: OpenAI also said last week it cut GPT-5.6 Luna pricing by 80 percent and Terra pricing by 20 percent, while adding a faster Sol mode in the API. The implementation lesson is model routing. Use cheaper models for high-volume extraction, tagging, summaries, and routine workflow steps when private evaluations prove quality. Use stronger or faster models where the cost of delay or error is higher: compliance review, coding, fraud triage, underwriting support, exception handling, and executive analysis.

HOST: The counter-signal is governance. Lower prices can increase uncontrolled usage, and live voice can increase trust before controls are mature. Watch whether vendors ship agent registries, permission maps, evaluation reports, incident controls, and cost dashboards as standard product features. The best enterprise A I programs will not pick one model and hope. They will route work, measure outcomes, and keep humans in the approval loop where judgment matters.

HOST: Markets are trying to extend Monday's rally, but the setup is less clean than it looked yesterday. AP reported the S and P 500 rose 1.5 percent Monday to 7,600.50, the Dow gained 693 points to a record 53,178.41, and the Nasdaq rose 2.1 percent. The 10-year Treasury yield fell to about 4.68 percent as oil dropped and inflation fear eased.

COHOST: This morning, futures are still pointed higher, but oil is bouncing because Hormuz risk is not settled.

HOST: That is the useful market signal. Stocks like lower oil, better manufacturing data, and big-tech leadership. But borrowers and businesses still need long yields to confirm the move. Watch Palantir's post-earnings reaction, A M D later today, SpaceX's first public earnings report after the close, and Friday's jobs data. The risk to the rally is that oil relief, A I earnings, and rate relief do not all hold at the same time.

HOST: For Columbus weather, it is a useful August day. Current conditions are clear and around 59 degrees. Today should be mostly sunny, with a high near 87 and a low around 65. Wednesday turns more humid with thick cloud cover and a couple of afternoon showers or a thunderstorm, high near 86. Thursday stays humid with intervals of clouds and sun and a thunderstorm in spots.

COHOST: For Central Ohio, use today for outdoor errands, work around the heat in the afternoon, and watch Wednesday if you have school prep, construction work, fair plans, or evening events.

HOST: The Tuesday watchlist is specific. One, whether the tariff lawsuit produces a fast request to pause collections. Two, whether the Hormuz ship incident changes naval posture or oil pricing. Three, what actually files for the November ballot in Franklin County by Wednesday. Four, whether Columbus council uses the Flock hearing to tighten data rules or question the contract itself. Five, whether Thursday's mortgage survey confirms any rate relief. And six, whether A I buyers start asking for latency, routing, permission, and audit evidence instead of treating live voice and cheaper models as stand-alone features.

COHOST: The practical theme is that institutions have to convert headlines into rules. Courts, shipping lanes, city councils, lenders, markets, and A I teams all have the same test this week: what can people safely do next?

HOST: That is your Morning Brief for Tuesday, August 4th. Have a good morning, and watch which signals become operating facts.

Good morning. It is Monday, August 3rd, 2026, and this is your Morning Brief.

COHOST: The frame today is risk reduction, not resolution. Washington is trying to avoid another shutdown. Markets are reacting to a pause in Iran strikes. Columbus has two days before a ballot deadline. Mortgage lenders are watching whether lower oil can ease rates. And A I companies are learning that agent control is not optional infrastructure.

HOST: Start in Washington, where the fresh development is a short-term spending deal. The Associated Press reports key senators unveiled a bill Sunday that would keep federal agencies funded at generally current levels through December 11th. The Senate is expected to vote before lawmakers leave for the August recess, and the point is timing: Congress is trying to remove a shutdown fight from the middle of campaign season, after two bruising shutdowns in the past ten months.

COHOST: The practical consequence is not that the budget problem is solved. It is that federal agencies, contractors, grant recipients, airports, national parks, and benefit administrators may get a few months of operating visibility.

HOST: Exactly. A continuing resolution is a bridge, not a budget. It keeps the lights on while pushing the hard decisions into December: defense spending, non-defense cuts, border funding, health insurance tax credits, and agency grant rules. The bill also reportedly leaves out a White House request for 1 billion dollars for Trump-class battleships and includes language Democrats say would stop the administration from moving money from other programs to the Border Patrol.

HOST: The affected parties are bigger than Congress. Federal workers want to know whether paychecks continue. Contractors want to know whether invoices get processed. States, universities, nonprofits, and local governments want to know whether federal grant flows remain predictable. Businesses want to avoid another confidence shock right before the fall selling season.

COHOST: The counter-signal is that passing a short-term bill early can also mean the real fight gets larger later. December becomes the new deadline.

HOST: That is the watch item. Follow whether the Senate passes the measure this week, whether the House accepts the Senate version, and whether agencies begin planning as if December 11th is the next fiscal cliff. The useful interpretation is that both parties have an incentive to avoid owning a shutdown before voters go to the polls, but they have not solved the spending conflict underneath it.

HOST: There is a second Washington story because it shows where Senate leverage still works. AP reports Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche issued a formal order late Sunday terminating President Trump's 1.8 billion dollar anti-weaponization fund, which was designed to compensate political allies. The move followed negotiations with two Republican senators who had been blocking Blanche's nomination to become attorney general. A Senate Judiciary Committee vote is expected Tuesday.

COHOST: That is a power-map story. The White House had the policy. Blanche needed the nomination. Two senators had procedural leverage. The fund became the bargaining chip.

HOST: Right. The practical consequence is institutional. Justice Department money, victim-compensation logic, and political grievance were getting tangled together. Rescinding the fund lowers one confirmation obstacle, but it also tells agencies and nominees that Senate factions can still extract concrete policy changes if the vote margin is tight. Watch Tuesday's committee vote, whether the order is durable, and whether Democrats use the episode to question Blanche about independence at the department.

HOST: The global swing factor is still the Middle East. President Trump said Sunday he would hold off on new U.S. strikes on Iran after Gulf allies urged more time for diplomacy. AP reports the emerging proposal would bring the U.S. and Iran back to negotiations, reopen the Strait of Hormuz, halt regional attacks by Iranian-backed militias, end the U.S. naval blockade on Iran, and allow Tehran to export oil under a tentative ceasefire framework.

COHOST: That is why oil moved immediately. If Hormuz risk falls, inflation pressure can fall with it.

HOST: Exactly. AP reported U.S. crude dropped about 5 percent to 80 dollars and 79 cents a barrel, while Brent fell to about 83 dollars and 87 cents. That matters for gasoline, jet fuel, shipping, trucking, manufacturing input costs, Treasury yields, mortgage rates, and central-bank expectations. The why-now is simple: markets had priced war risk into energy, and now they are testing whether diplomacy deserves a discount.

HOST: The counter-signal is strong. Iran's Foreign Ministry said the Strait of Hormuz will not simply return to its prewar status, and AP notes Trump has announced strike pauses before only for fighting to resume. Israel also had not publicly endorsed the Iran announcement when AP reported it. So the market can get relief before the facts are secure.

COHOST: Gaza is connected because the same regional trust problem appears there.

HOST: Israel said it has serious concerns with the Hamas disarmament deal. AP also reported Israeli strikes killed Palestinians in Gaza over the weekend, even as the U.S.-backed plan is supposed to connect Hamas weapons steps, Israeli withdrawal, international verification, and a stabilization force. The practical consequence is humanitarian and operational: aid routes, border control, reconstruction, hostage and detainee talks, and regional force commitments all depend on verified sequence.

HOST: For listeners, the important distinction is between announcement risk and verification risk. A headline can say deal. Operations require named monitors, a weapons-transfer mechanism, a strike pause, a withdrawal calendar, and outside governments willing to put personnel and money behind the plan. Watch whether talks actually restart today, whether any first weapons step is verified, whether oil keeps falling, and whether shipping through Hormuz becomes real instead of aspirational.

HOST: In Central Ohio, the local story is the August 5th ballot deadline. W O S U reported Columbus State Community College ended its effort to place a Franklin County property-tax levy on the November ballot to fund free tuition. COHOST: That is a different risk than a chatbot giving a bad answer. It is an agent taking actions in connected systems.

HOST: Exactly. For banks, mortgage companies, healthcare firms, governments, and large enterprises, the lesson is not to ban useful A I. Good morning. It is Sunday, August 2nd, 2026, and this is your Morning Brief.

COHOST: The frame today is systems under stress. Water utilities are dealing with cyber risk, Middle East diplomacy is trying to turn announcements into verification, Columbus is testing civic capacity, mortgage lenders are testing borrower math, and A I buyers are testing whether cheaper models can stay governed.

HOST: Start nationally with a story that sounds technical but is very practical. The Associated Press reports Michigan has joined Minnesota in reporting cyberattacks on water systems. Michigan officials said nine systems were affected and were operating safely. Minnesota said more than 30 community water systems were targeted earlier in the week, with disruptions involving remote monitoring and control systems.

COHOST: The key point is that this is not a consumer-data breach. It touches operational technology, meaning the equipment and software that helps run public infrastructure.

HOST: Exactly. AP says the F B I and federal partners are investigating, and attribution has not been formally established. That uncertainty matters. There are suspicions around foreign actors because federal alerts have warned about attempts to tamper with water-system technology, and Iranian-linked hackers have shown interest in U.S. infrastructure before. But the responsible way to understand this this morning is narrower: multiple local water systems have been probed or disrupted, public-health officials say the affected systems are safe, and federal investigators are still working on who did it and how widely it spread.

HOST: The affected parties are local utilities, city managers, ratepayers, hospitals, schools, businesses, and households that assume water is boring because it usually works. The practical consequence is budget and resilience. Many small and midsize utilities do not have large cyber teams. They may rely on remote access, older industrial controls, vendors, and stretched municipal staff. A cyberattack that only causes a temporary shutdown is still a warning that manual fallback plans, network segmentation, password hygiene, vendor access, and emergency communications are now local-government necessities.

COHOST: The counter-signal is important too. Officials are not saying drinking water was poisoned or that every water system is vulnerable in the same way. Panic is not useful. Operational preparedness is.

HOST: Right. Watch whether C I S A, the F B I, E P A, or state agencies issue a broader advisory; whether more states disclose incidents; and whether local utilities begin telling residents what controls they have in place. The unusually useful takeaway is that critical infrastructure risk is increasingly a local management problem, not just a federal-security problem.

HOST: The second national pressure point is the Middle East, where there are two fresh developments and both depend on follow-through. AP reports Palestinians in Gaza are reacting with hope and deep skepticism after President Trump announced that Hamas agreed to disarm under a U.S.-backed plan. The plan is supposed to connect Hamas weapons steps, Israeli withdrawal, international verification, a stabilization force, and a new Palestinian administrative body.

COHOST: So the story is no longer just whether a deal was announced. It is whether anyone can prove the first step happened.

HOST: Exactly. Palestinians in Gaza want strikes to end and rebuilding to begin. Israeli leaders want security guarantees, demilitarization, and political cover. Hamas says later heavy-weapons steps are tied to Israeli withdrawal and Palestinian statehood. International backers would have to supply monitors, police or troops, money, and legitimacy. The practical consequence is enormous: aid delivery, reconstruction, border operations, hostage and detainee negotiations, and regional security could change if even the first phase holds.

HOST: The counter-signal is that trust is still the scarcest resource. AP reports Israeli strikes have continued, Israel has not provided the kind of uncomplicated public acceptance that would make implementation automatic, and full disarmament could take many months. Watch for verified weapons transfer, a real pause in strikes, named stabilization-force commitments, and a public Israeli calendar.

COHOST: Iran is the other clock. A Gaza process can be pulled off course quickly if Gulf security, oil shipping, or militia attacks flare again.

HOST: That is why AP's other fresh report matters. President Trump said he would halt planned U.S. strikes on Iran after Middle Eastern allies reached outlines of a possible deal to end the Iran war, including reopening the Strait of Hormuz and returning to negotiations. The practical market consequence is direct: fewer strikes could relieve oil and shipping pressure, but only if Iran, Israel, Gulf governments, and the U.S. can turn a pause into enforceable behavior.

HOST: In Central Ohio, the local story is civic capacity, with a weekend overlay. W O S U reported this week that Columbus stopped plans for a new Franklin County Municipal Court building after projected costs rose above 335 million dollars. Mayor Andrew Ginther defended the renovation path, saying the city could spend about 260 million dollars renovating the current complex and redirect 75 million dollars elsewhere.

COHOST: That is not just a courthouse story. It is a signal about how expensive public construction has become and how many priorities are now competing for the same tax capacity.

HOST: Right. The affected parties are court users, judges, city taxpayers, downtown workers, neighborhood advocates, and anyone waiting for basic capital projects. The practical consequence is prioritization. If a new court building can move from 200 million dollars in the old estimate to more than 335 million today, every future ask for schools, roads, public safety facilities, parks, housing infrastructure, and neighborhood investment faces tougher scrutiny.

HOST: The same constraint is visible in Columbus State's decision to drop its proposed Franklin County free-tuition levy while keeping Columbus Promise available for current students, fall entrants, and the class of 2027. The useful local interpretation is that good ideas still need durable funding. The counter-signal is that pausing can be responsible if leaders do not yet have a voter-ready plan. The watch item is the August 5 ballot-filing deadline, replacement-funding talks, and whether city leaders put firmer renovation numbers in front of the public.

COHOST: And today, local operations are literal. Pelotonia, the Ohio State Fair, the Dublin Irish Festival, Gallery Hop spillover, concerts, and storms all compete for roads, police, volunteers, vendors, and family calendars.

HOST: Exactly. For Central Ohio listeners, plan around traffic, wet roads, and event timing. These events are good for civic life and local business, but they also show how quickly weather and logistics can turn a normal weekend into an operating test.

HOST: In home lending and mortgage, the fresh issue is not just that rates are high. It is that they have moved enough to force requalification. Freddie Mac's July 30 survey put the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage at 6.66 percent, up from 6.58 percent the prior week, and the 15-year at 6.04 percent. Freddie Mac releases that survey on Thursdays, and AP notes the 30-year average is at its highest level in a year. M B A data showed mortgage applications fell 6.4 percent for the week ending July 24.

COHOST: The borrower impact is immediate. A buyer who qualified two weeks ago may need a new payment conversation before making an offer or clearing conditions.

HOST: Exactly. The affected parties are purchase borrowers, loan officers, processors, real estate agents, builders, secondary desks, and servicers trying to keep customers warm. The practical consequence is pipeline triage. Reconfirm debt-to-income ratios. Refresh taxes, insurance, dues, points, and cash-to-close assumptions. Separate borrowers who should lock from those who need seller credits, builder incentives, a smaller price point, a temporary buydown, or a longer nurture path.

HOST: For lenders, the operational move is to turn uncertainty into triggers. Do not tell a refinance lead, we will call when rates improve. Give the borrower a specific payment, rate, and break-even threshold. For purchase leads, compare permanent points with temporary buydowns using expected time in the home and realistic refinance probability. For builders, incentives should be measured by conversion and cancellation rates, not by how attractive the flyer looks.

COHOST: The counter-signal is inventory and concessions. More listings can still help buyers if sellers participate in solving the payment problem.

HOST: Right. Watch the 10-year Treasury, daily lender sheets, next week's M B A purchase-versus-refinance split, and whether seller credits start doing more work than list-price cuts. The mortgage market is saying affordability is not one number. It is rate, income, inventory, concessions, insurance, and confidence all at once.

HOST: In A I and technology, the practical story is price-performance. OpenAI says it cut GPT-5.6 Luna prices by 80 percent and Terra prices by 20 percent, while adding Fast mode for GPT-5.6 Sol in the API. Fast mode is described as up to two and a half times faster than standard processing at twice the price, with no change in model intelligence.

COHOST: That changes how enterprises should buy A I. The question is not which model is best in the abstract. It is which model is right for each workflow.

HOST: Exactly. Luna-type economics favor high-volume extraction, tagging, summaries, simple customer-service drafts, and back-office automations. Terra-type models fit everyday knowledge work where cost and quality both matter. Sol Fast mode is for latency-sensitive work where waiting changes the outcome: live service recovery, analyst support, coding loops, sales enablement, incident response, and time-sensitive document review.

HOST: The practical consequence for banks, mortgage companies, and large enterprises is model routing. A governed A I program should know which task goes to which model, what data is allowed, who approves actions, how outputs are audited, and what metric improves. The counter-signal is that lower prices can create more uncontrolled usage. Cheaper intelligence only helps if cost controls, access controls, evaluation sets, and human review improve at the same time.

COHOST: The latest model update from Google DeepMind pushes that governance question into physical space.

HOST: Google DeepMind introduced Gemini Robotics 2 for whole-body robot control, dexterity, and multi-robot collaboration, along with ASIMOV-Agentic, a benchmark for agentic safety and uncertainty handling. The useful distinction is that robotics A I is not only about understanding instructions. It is about whether a machine should move, stop, ask for help, or refuse an unsafe action around people and property.

HOST: The workflows are warehouses, inspection, light manufacturing, labs, facilities, elder-care support, and logistics. The implementation model is physical: human proximity rules, environment mapping, maintenance logs, incident review, insurance, cyber controls, and a clear kill switch. The counter-signal is that demos are still not broad deployment. Watch developer access, hardware partners, and whether safety benchmarks become procurement requirements rather than launch-day decoration.

HOST: Markets are closed today, so use Friday's close as the snapshot. AP reported the S and P 500 rose 0.7 percent to 7,489.72, the Dow gained 0.5 percent to 52,485.03, and the Nasdaq rose 1 percent to 25,373.85. Amazon jumped after profit more than tripled and cloud growth supported the A I spending case. Apple fell after a softer revenue-growth outlook. Brent crude settled around 87 dollars and 93 cents, and the 10-year Treasury yield was around 4.71 percent.

COHOST: The market signal is split. Stocks liked evidence that A I capex can produce revenue. Bonds are still warning that oil, inflation, and policy uncertainty can keep borrowing costs high.

HOST: That matters for investors and borrowers at the same time. If long yields stay high, stock valuations, mortgage rates, auto loans, credit costs, and federal interest expense all feel it. Watch whether the Iran pause pulls oil down, whether Treasury yields follow, and whether upcoming earnings from A M D, Palantir, Disney, and Eli Lilly broaden the market story beyond the biggest tech platforms.

HOST: For Columbus weather, it is a humid and flexible-plans day. Current conditions are mostly cloudy around 72 degrees. Expect a cloudy morning, some sun this afternoon, a high near 79, and a couple of showers or a thunderstorm. Ponding on roads is possible. Monday stays humid with intervals of clouds and sun and a high near 81. Tuesday is partly sunny and humid with a couple of afternoon thundershowers and a high near 84.

COHOST: For Pelotonia, the fair, festival traffic, errands, and outdoor meals, keep rain gear close, watch radar before you leave, and give yourself more stopping distance if heavier cells move through.

HOST: The Sunday watchlist is specific. One, whether federal investigators expand the water-system cyber warning beyond Michigan and Minnesota. Two, whether Gaza produces verified first steps rather than more statements. Three, whether the Iran pause lowers oil and Treasury pressure. Four, whether Columbus leaders clarify funding before the August 5 ballot deadline. Five, whether mortgage lenders adjust pipelines before stale preapprovals become failed transactions. And six, whether A I buyers treat price cuts as a routing and governance problem, not just a cheaper-token headline.

COHOST: The common thread is that resilience now has to be operational. Cybersecurity, diplomacy, public budgets, mortgage qualification, model routing, and weather planning all come down to whether the system works when pressure hits.

HOST: That is your Morning Brief for Sunday, August 2nd. Have a good morning, and watch the practical tests behind the headlines.

COHOST: The common thread is execution. Announcements are easy. Verification, funding, qualification, governance, and measurable results are the harder tests.

HOST: That is your Morning Brief for Saturday, August 1st. Have a good morning, and watch what turns promises into working systems.

item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It is Friday, July 31st, 2026, and this is your Morning Brief.

COHOST: The frame today is proof under pressure. The economy has growth, but not clean growth. A I has capability, but not clean control. Housing has inventory, but not cheap financing. And Ohio politics has attention, but not much quiet.

HOST: Start with the national economy, because yesterday's data gave the Fed a complicated picture, not a simple green light. The Associated Press reports the U.S. economy grew at a 1.5 percent annual pace in the second quarter. That is slower than the 2.1 percent pace in the first quarter and below expectations. But the details are less weak than the headline: consumer spending rose at a 3.2 percent annual rate, and a measure of underlying domestic demand grew 3.9 percent.

COHOST: So the headline says slowdown, but the inside of the report says households and businesses are still moving.

HOST: Exactly. The drag was imports. Imports rose at an 11.5 percent pace, and because G D P counts domestic production, imports subtract from the number. AP says part of that import surge came from chips and other products supporting A I investment. Business investment outside housing was still strong, up at an 8.4 percent pace. That matters because A I is no longer just a stock-market theme. It is showing up as real capital spending, supply-chain demand, data-center construction, power demand, and imported hardware.

HOST: The practical consequence is that policymakers and executives cannot treat this as a normal soft-growth report. Consumers are still spending. Businesses are still investing. But the economy is absorbing higher borrowing costs, higher energy risk from the Iran war, and still-elevated prices.

COHOST: The counter-signal is inflation. The P C E price index eased from May, but it did not get close to the Fed's 2 percent target.

HOST: Right. The Commerce Department's P C E index rose 3.7 percent from a year earlier in June, down from 4.1 percent in May. Core P C E was 3.3 percent, little changed from 3.4 percent. Prices fell month to month because gasoline and other energy products dropped in June, but that relief came before the newest Iran escalation and oil rebound. That is why the Fed's Wednesday hold still matters this morning. The target range stayed at 3.5 to 3.75 percent, but three Fed officials dissented in favor of a hike.

HOST: Who is affected? Households with grocery, gas, rent, and credit-card exposure. Employers planning wages. Retailers watching real spending power. Builders and lenders watching rates. And investors trying to decide whether A I capital spending can offset inflation pressure. What could weaken the hawkish interpretation is another clean inflation report and lower oil. What strengthens it is energy passing through to goods, freight, airfare, and expectations. Watch July jobs, oil, and Fed speakers before Jackson Hole.

HOST: In Washington, one political development sharpens the same national story. The Senate narrowly rejected a war-powers effort to halt Trump's Iran hostilities, with the resolution failing 49 to 50. That does not end the conflict, and it does not end congressional pressure. It shows the administration still has room to operate, but the margin is thin enough that every oil spike, attack on U.S. forces, or new cost estimate can change the politics quickly.

COHOST: The useful takeaway is that the Iran story now has three clocks: the military clock, the energy-price clock, and the congressional clock.

HOST: Exactly. The next watch item is whether the White House can define an end state before lawmakers, voters, or fuel prices define one for it.

HOST: In Central Ohio, the freshest local operating story is political attention and money. Axios Columbus reports political groups are expected to spend about 750 million dollars in Ohio this election cycle, according to AdImpact's 2026 report. That is 70 percent above the initial forecast and puts Ohio fourth nationally in projected ad spending, behind California, Michigan, and Texas.

COHOST: That matters locally because Columbus is not just watching the midterms. It is one of the places where turnout, messaging, and media saturation will be fought hardest.

HOST: Right. Axios notes Ohio's three C cities are the largest Democratic strongholds, and both parties see major races here: Sherrod Brown against appointed Republican Senator Jon Husted, Amy Acton against Vivek Ramaswamy for governor, and redrawn House races that could affect control of Congress. For Columbus listeners, the practical consequence is not only more commercials. It is pressure on local news inventory, digital ad costs, campaign field hiring, ballot education, and voter fatigue right as local tax issues and public-safety debates also need attention.

HOST: The counter-signal is that ad spending does not equal persuasion. It can mobilize, but it can also numb voters. The more operational watch item is turnout. Axios points to May primary turnout where the parties nearly matched after Republican voters had outnumbered Democrats almost two to one in the 2022 May primary. Watch whether Columbus and Franklin County become a turnout engine, whether the October 5 registration deadline becomes a major organizing marker, and whether local ballot questions get drowned out by national messaging.

HOST: Also keep the Columbus civic calendar in view. The Ohio State Fair is underway, and Axios reports two Freedom 250 attractions from the Trump administration's national initiative are coming to the fair: the Freedom Ferris Wheel and mobile museum trucks. That is lighter than tax policy, but it fits the same attention story. The fair is a family event, a traffic event, and this year also a national-message event. The practical note is to expect crowds around the fairgrounds and more political texture than usual.

HOST: In home lending and mortgage, the fresh number is Freddie Mac's Thursday update. The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 6.66 percent as of July 30, up from 6.58 percent the prior week. The 15-year averaged 6.04 percent, up from 5.96 percent. Freddie Mac says the housing market continues to benefit from more available inventory, but the rate move puts that inventory into a harder affordability box.

COHOST: That is the mortgage tension right now: more choices for buyers, but a payment calculation that keeps getting less forgiving.

HOST: Exactly. This is the highest 30-year Freddie Mac average in a year, and it follows the M B A report showing applications fell 6.4 percent last week. For borrowers, the operational issue is not whether 6.66 sounds high in the abstract. It is whether the loan still qualifies after taxes, insurance, dues, points, and cash to close. For loan officers, the issue is pipeline triage. Who needs a lock now? Who needs seller credits? Who can use builder incentives? Who should compare temporary buydowns against permanent points? And who is really a nurture lead until rates or income change?

HOST: The counter-signal is inventory. More listings can create room for concessions, and some households can still transact if sellers participate in the financing solution. But higher Treasury yields and a divided Fed reduce the chance of quick rate relief. The watch item is whether the 10-year Treasury cools after the P C E report, whether lenders keep spreads tight to defend volume, and whether next week's M B A report shows buyers adapting or stepping back.

COHOST: For mortgage leaders, this is also a communication test. Vague refinance promises are weaker than a written trigger tied to rate, payment, and break-even math.

HOST: In A I and technology, the newest model story is physical. Google DeepMind introduced Gemini Robotics 2, a model family for whole-body robot control, fine dexterity, and multi-robot teamwork. Google says the system is meant to move robots beyond tabletop demonstrations toward coordinated movement from feet to fingertips. Reporting from W I R E D says the system combines models that understand vision and language with vision-language-action models that control full-body movement, hands, and grippers.

COHOST: That changes the enterprise question. A chatbot can make a bad recommendation. A robot can move through a warehouse, clinic, lab, store, or home.

HOST: Exactly. The practical workflows are not here for every company tomorrow, but the direction matters: warehouse handling, inspection, light manufacturing, elder-care assistance, facilities work, lab operations, and defense logistics. The implementation model is very different from deploying a document copilot. Companies need physical safety boundaries, human proximity detection, task approvals, environment mapping, maintenance controls, incident logs, and insurance review. Google is also introducing an ASIMOV-Agentic benchmark for robot safety, which is the right kind of signal: capability releases need evaluation systems that match the risk surface.

HOST: The counter-signal is that demonstrations are still demonstrations. W I R E D notes the models are trained through simulations, video examples, and human teleoperation, and robots still need specific training for complex real-world tasks. The next watch item is access: which developers can use the models, which robot bodies can run them reliably, and whether safety benchmarks catch enough edge cases before robots work around people.

HOST: The second A I signal is less flashy but just as practical. Axios reports Scale A I hired Google Cloud C O O Francis deSouza as chief executive. Scale built its business on data and human evaluations for model training, but Axios says the company is expanding into enterprise and government A I applications, and its applications business is expected to overtake its data business within 18 months.

COHOST: That is a useful enterprise tell. The money is moving from training data alone toward deployment infrastructure, evaluation, and business outcomes.

HOST: Exactly. For banks, mortgage companies, insurers, and large employers, the takeaway is that A I value is migrating into the operating layer: private evaluations, workflow integration, governance evidence, human review queues, model routing, data permissions, and measurable cost or cycle-time improvement. The risk is vendor sprawl. Every platform will claim it can turn pilots into production. The buyer's job is to ask which system of record it touches, what data it needs, who owns failure, and what metric improves.

HOST: Markets gave A I investors a rebound, but not a clean all-clear. AP reports the S and P 500 rose 1.7 percent Thursday, the Dow gained 613 points, or 1.2 percent, and the Nasdaq jumped 2.8 percent. Microsoft rose 15.5 percent, its best day since 2008, after earnings reassured investors about cloud growth and A I spending. Chip names rebounded too.

COHOST: But the bond market did not give the same relaxed signal.

HOST: Right. Long-term inflation worries remain, and the rally was still heavily tied to a few A I leaders. This morning, futures looked higher after Amazon's strong results, while Apple weakened after guidance concerns. The assumption being priced is that A I capex can produce enough revenue to justify the buildout. What could weaken that assumption is higher long-term yields, oil pressure, narrow market breadth, or earnings that show spending rising faster than useful demand.

HOST: For Columbus weather, today is mostly sunny and warm, with a high near 88 and a low around 68. Current conditions are mostly cloudy around 64. Saturday turns humid, not as warm, and brings the bigger planning risk: a heavy thunderstorm in the afternoon. Sunday stays humid with showers and a thunderstorm possible.

COHOST: So today is the better fair and outdoor day. For the weekend, build plans around afternoon storm flexibility, not just heat.

HOST: The Friday watchlist is specific. One, whether oil and July data push the Fed's divided hold closer to a September hike. Two, whether Ohio's record ad market turns Columbus into a turnout engine or just a saturated media market. Three, whether mortgage lenders can convert borrowers with concessions and lock discipline while the 30-year sits at 6.66 percent. Four, whether Google can turn robotics safety benchmarks into deployable controls. Five, whether Scale A I's enterprise turn signals a broader shift from model demos to governed production. And six, whether the market's A I rebound broadens beyond the biggest winners.

COHOST: The common thread is that the easy headline is less useful than the operating test: who pays, who controls the risk, who can measure the result, and what changes next.

HOST: That is your Morning Brief for Friday, July 31st. Have a good morning, and watch the proof behind the promise.
